entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Herat  Mileage = 35270 (7670 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In the morning, after getting some money, we drove off to Herat.  Fred stopped, and our bicycling friend came up, he and Dad fiddled a bit and then Fred started again.  We drove into Herat, it was a dirt track in between mud(?) houses, we stopped to buy the first bread in Afghanistan, and some fruit.  We drove past lots of small shops and out onto a big square, we went onto a tarmac road, and started looking for a campsite.  We stopped in a park for lunch, and then went to look for the bazaar, resolving to find a campsite afterwards.  We never actually found the bazaar but the people were interesting.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We got some money and set off to Herat. We passed an English bicyclist, who had had coffee with us last night. He had been through Africa, Greece, Turkey and Iran, and was just starting on Afghanistan. We gave him a Change of Address card. We went on a bit when Fred broke down, so we had a coffee, then the man on the bike came, so dad and him had a go on the engine. They fixed it and we went to Herat.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We got some money from ye bank.  We started to go to Herat.  We saw the bicyclist and broke down.  When we were going again we saw some camels then Mum and Dad and Denise went and visited some windmills.  When we reached Herat and had a look around a bazaar we went to a Hotel see ??? at ???

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We found a Hotel, called the ‘Salang Hotel’ and we camped in it’s garden, they had an enormous pelican and two ducks.  In the morning we all had hot showers, the water was heated by an old boiler, and we had to keep wood in it.  In the morning we washed clothes, and tidied Fred, then Mum & Dad rushed off to the bank, only to find that it is closed at 12.00, not 1.00.  We had lunch and then went out, taking our old radio with us.  We walked up the main street, there were lots of fur and leather shops there, I tried on some sheepskin jackets, but they had been very badly cured, and they were smelly.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Most of the streets in Herat are not tarmacked and are very bumpy. Along the main street there were lots of fur shops. I liked the leopard skins most. Mum wouldn’t let us buy anything though I wanted to buy some small scraps to polish things, I mean shine things, like our shield and helmet, etc. They all had some furry tails, which I liked especially. Then we went to lots of looms. They were weaving silk. Most looms were operated by foot and hand. Then we went back to the campsite.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: Music.  We left Herat and went to a graveyard where there was a very old and famous pistachio tree with lots of nails in it.  Women were meant to tie pieces of string to it and set fire to them if they wanted a child.  We met a nice man in a white coat who showed us the tombs of black marble which had taken 12 ears to carve and 7 chisels.  After that we went to a shop where Mum had bought 7 beads and D bought 3.  We were there to hear some music which was played by the shopkeeper on a sort of loot (sic) and a drum which looked like this. (Pic)

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: The shop was very interesting.  Herat has no tarmac roads but lots of horse and carriages.  The horses have lots of red bomboms on then and some had bells.  There are lots of hotels as well.  Herat has a Friday Mosque.  There are lots of weavers who weave silk on looms.  The looms are in rooms side by side that you can see into.  All the looms had horse hair on them.  Men wove using both hand and foot.  The silk was bright patterns.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Met a bicyclist called ‘David’, very nice.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: When we woke up, Francis and I went to get the bread, I wore my chouda.  After breakfast, we went to visit the Friday Mosque, we went in, and up a corridor, til we came to a big courtyard, we took off our shows, then a policeman came and said we could come back in the afternoon, so we went out.  We looked at some shops, and Dad found some lovely red beads, they were very expensive though.  We looked in some other shops, and Francis found some more beads, but they weren’t in a necklace.  Mum and Dad chose some, and the old man said they were 70 Afs.  Dad said 60, but the man wouldn’t budge.  We were just going, when he said, OK 60, and he gave me some beads as well, then he said, come back at 4.00 for chai and music.  When we came, after seeing a beautiful carved black marble stone, he played a stringed instrument and his brother played on a skin drum.  We recorded it, it was super.  After listening to the music, it was too late to go to Kandahar, so we stayed at the ‘Salang’ another night.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We had a quick look at the mosque then went to some shops. There were some nice helmets. One had a flat cow head with bits of glass on for eyes, etc. Also the shields were well decorated with nice bits of metal and knobs. I went on to another shop and found some red glass beads with calligraphy on. The man said it had something to do with Allah. We bought a few. (pic)

entries.speaker: Mum
entries.text: pilgrim beads. Nice men came and played music for an hour with us just for friendship.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Farahrod  Mileage = 35872 (8272 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In the morning we drove off and Mum & Dad visited the Friday Mosque and H & I visited some shops, looking for mascara jar, in one shop, the man gave us both a ring for ‘Baksheesh’ (gift).

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We went and had lunch in a park, just out of town, we were just about to drive out, when Dad remembered the blue glass beads that we saw, so, back we went!  We bought 3 strings of beads.  And then at last, we got on the road to Kandahar.  We drove through lots of scrub/desert and small mountains, there were lots of Nomad tents and camels.  At last we found a place to camp, it was near a dried up river bed, in the bank, F, H & I dug some caves, for the Villas, Hills, Oppies and Us, the bank was about two feet higher than me.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: D and I went and did some shopping in the nearest shops looking for mascara jars.  We didn’t like any we saw but in the last shop a man gave D and I a ring each and one bead to me.  At our campsite there was a dried up river which had a clay cliff about two feet higher than D in one place.  We dug some small and some big caves to miniature soldier scale.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 35933 (8333 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36071 Bost (8471 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We’ve seen lots and lots of camels and nomads etc - it was difficult to find a spot to camp, free from them.  We saw the beginnings of sand dunes.  We also saw some big mirages of lakes and things.  We turned a corner, and the ground was covered by pink flowers, they were small, dry pink bubbles on spikey little plants, we drove on a bit, and then there were none.  Beautiful sunset.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We went to see some ruins as ‘Bost’ there were at least 2 miles of ruins, it used to be a Winter Palace, about 900 years ago.  There was a super gateway, at the foot of a small fortified hill, we climbed up, and then down, underground, the descent was difficult as there was lots of rubble, an Afghan took us down.  We forded a river, there was an interesting little foot bridge.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We left Herat and went along semi-desert. Then turned onto a grit road. It was very dusty; everything got covered with dust. There were lots of nomads and camels with big flocks. We forded a river or two. They had concrete so that we would not bog down. The water made a nice noise on the tyres. Then we drove to some ruins; they used to be a summer palace. Then we went on a bit to the restored arch of Bost. It was near a fortified hill and within the fort’s walls up on the hill there were lots of big walls (as well as those on the ground).The hill had a deep hole with lots of rooms on either side [pic]. Someone said they were dungeons. We went in. Two people followed us. There were lots of little hard squiggly black things, like this [pic]. They ponged like nothing on earth. We thought the holes were not dungeons but places where people lived. Some were dark. In one place the tunnel was dark and on a slope with only rubble and lots of sand-dust. We kept on falling and choking in the dust we kicked up.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: When we forded the big river there was a small foot suspension bridge [pic]. It swayed in the wind. The water was very clear. A boy was fishing from the bridge. The water made a nice noise against the tyres.  On the way back from the ruins to the non-grit road we had a blow-out. There was a big hole in the tyre.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Helena and I went to look at a camel. He had a blanket with a hole in it. The hole was for his hump. (pic)

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We saw a fortified hill near the Arch of Bost.  From the top, we went down down down to the bottom of a building which was inside the hill.

entries.speaker: Mum
entries.text: Shaft joins a waterway.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We drove on and on, on a dirt track, until we had a blow out, it was one of the new tyres, we changed it and then drove on, until at last we got onto the smooth main road.  After an hours or two’s driving, we entered Kandahar.  We bought some bread, and then drove off to a park for lunch, that Fodor mentions, it was miles away, over a small mountain pass, when we got there it was nice though.  After lunch, we drove back into Kandahar to see the throne of ‘Babul’ (first of the great Moguls), it had 42 steps leading up to it (puff, pant).  We found a Bakerie, selling doughnuts, and apple pies, and other delicious things, it also sold Hard cheese, we spent just under £2.00 there - man - delicious!  We stayed in a campsite.  H & I had a lovely hot shower.  We had cauliflower cheese for dinner.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We were driving into Kandahar when we were told to stop by some soldiers so we stopped. A bit later two tanks came, and an armoured car, so mum got the camera ready in case some more might come, then three tanks and an armoured car. So Mum took a photo of a tank and an armoured car. The tanks had their turrets the wrong way round. (pic)

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We went to the throne of Babul. It was carved out of the rock, the stairs were quite big, like this, but luckily it had railings on either side of the stairs, otherwise I don’t think I would have got up.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We went to the Bakshish Bakery and bought a big round flat thing, an apple pastie and a doughnut.  It is called Bakshish Bakery because bakshish means free gift and the baker gave us things to taste.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: When we climbed the throne of Baba Soab - which had 46 steep steps - we got very tired so we sat at the top and admired the super view of Kandahar. (Pic)

entries.speaker: Mum
entries.text: One side of the shovel digs in and the other side digs it out.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We met a man called Colin in a Landrover, a girl called Miranda was travelling with him from Tehran.  We went into town, Dad went to the Tyre shop, but it was closed, so Mum drove back to the Hotel to ask the tyre-man’s brother (who owned the Hotel) what was happening.  Dad waited by the tyre shop, and F, H & I went to the ‘Baksheesh Bakerie’ again, we spent 18 Afs, between us.  We got back to Dad, and soon the tyre man came, with the tyre, mended.  From the shop, we phoned Mum, she has having trouble with the car, so we hailed a Taxi (tiny 3 wheeled approx 5 seater) and us 4 plus a mechanic, the driver and a tyre squeezed in and drove to the Hotel.  While everyone fiddled with the car, F, H & I had eggs and chips in the restaurant, delicious chips.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We went to get the tyre but the shop was closed, so us children went to a bakery and bought some food to munch while we waited for the tyre to be vulcanised. When we got it we went into a taxi and drove to Kandahar.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We were in the Aria Hotel.  Denise, Daddy, Francis and I went to town and all us children went to the bakshish bakery.  We bought several things and then went back to the tyre shop where Daddy was waiting for it to open.  Quite soon it opened.  We went back to the Hotel in a bubble taxi, 5 of us, a tyre and the driver.  The bubble taxi had three wheels.  I had to sit on Denise’s lap.  We had egg and chips for lunch in the hotel restaurant and told a ghost story which we called the Curse of the Green Hands.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36184 (8584 miles travelled) Kandahar

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36337 (8737 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36494 (8894 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Colin and Miranda slept in a hotel just up the road, as the Aria(?) was full, they left very early in the morning.  We fiddled about, and then drove to Kabul, it was a long drive, and on the way, we stopped at a town called ‘Ghazni’, we visited the Museum, it was in a small, old building, that the archeologists had restored.  Then we went to see the two very old minarets, they had beautiful carved stones, but were badly weathered.  We left Ghazni and drove on, but it soon began to get dark, we couldn’t find anywhere to camp, so in the end, we drove on to Kabul, in the dark it was difficult to find our way about, we got diddled at a petrol station.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We drove all morning, not even stopping for lunch! Then we went to Ghasni. It had a citadel with big mud walls on. We got a photo then we went to the museum. It has lots of pictures carved into big slabs of rock. They had some lions with ladies heads. Also there were lots of boars or wolves and lots of proper people, mostly warriors with swords and shields and spears. They looked to be hunting. Then we went to Kabul. It is a big city: the capital of Afghanistan.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: By the time we left the man had not arrived with Francis’ turban and cap and when we drove through the bazaar we looked for him but did not see him.  After that we drove and drove and drove not even stopping for lunch which was bread and dates and grapes.  When we got to Ghazni, we saw lots of ruins and then went to the museum.  At the museum there was a carving of an elephant - like this (Pic).

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We camped in the ‘Jam’ hotel and it certainly was a jam, there were 3 loos in between about 60 people, they were quite clean though.  In the morning, I washed a few clothes, and then we left.  Mum and Dad went round banks etc. but our maps seemed to bear very little relation to the actual streets.  We went back to ther Jam, and went to the loo.  Then we had a look at the Government shop nearby.  I found a super fur waistcoat for 350 afs.  Then we walked down ‘Chicken Street’.  We found ‘The Steakhouse’ so we had lunch there, it was delicious, there was free soup, as well.  It only cost 176 Afs (just under £3.00).  Then we just walked around Chicken Street, Dad bought a flowery waistcoat.  We went to find somewhere less crowded to camp, we looked in at the ‘Friends Hotel’, and guess who, Colin and Miranda were there.  Miranda had very bad tummy trouble.  We decided to stay there, with them, but it wasn’t very nice.  Then we drove around some more.  In another hotel we met Sharon, Dave and Kerry!  H & I saw some lovely little waistcoats, about Sasha doll size.  We are thinking of buying some waistcoats.  We bought some flowers for Miranda and surprisingly, I could bargain then down.  With the leftover money I bought her some biscuits.  We went back to the Hotel and talked.  Then, leaving Mum with Miranda, Colin, Dad, H, F and I went to the steakhouse for a hamburger.  After the meat course, Colin bought us all fresh strawberries and cream (- Dad) they were scrumptious!  On the way back we bought some lovely ginger snaps etc .

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Us children had a look in some government shops. I found a fur-lined waistcoat. It was not embroidered, so it didn’t cost much. We thought it was quite well cured but did not buy it because we were going to come back. Then we walked down Chicken Street. There were some nicely embroidered waistcoats. Dad got one.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36554 (8954 miles travelled) Chanrikar

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Camped at Bamyan.  Water pump broke.  Rained during night.  Snow on high mountains.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We drove through a river gorge. It was very fertile. All the trees had yellow leaves because of The Autumn. Once a little furry thing ran across the road.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: There were some mountains with snow on either side of the gorge, I wanted to climb up to them but Mum wouldn’t let us because it was very cold outside. And there were lots of people who might be unfriends.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: In the morning we went to a government shop which was very expensive.  There was a wood part and one part and a clothes part.  F saw a super waistcoat.  We walked down Chicken Street and saw lots of interesting clothes and brass shops - most of them had waistcoats in them.  At last we had lunch at the steakhouse.  (THINK THIS IS REALLY THURS 28 OCT).

entries.speaker: Mum
entries.text: Off road to Bamiyan was lovely.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36660 (9060 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Smudge’s Birthday

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In the morning we left quite early to go on the long drive to Bamiyan.  The scenery was beautiful, we could see lots of high, snow covered mountains, but the valleys were very fertile.  We rounded a corner, and saw a cliff face, riddled with caves, we drove on a bit and came into a small village, it was Bamiyan.  We stayed in posh, expensive hotel.  Beautiful view, but no water.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: When we woke up there was no water at all so we told the manager but still no water came; only steam out of the hot taps so, hurray, Hurray! We couldn't have a shower. Then we went to the citadel. There was one place where it had not been destroyed by Ghengis Khan. It had domes and plaster inside. I jumped in by a hole in the roof; they weren’t joined inside only outside. We had lunch and went to see the giant Buddas and caves. In one, plaster was made to look like wooden pillars. You had to go through a small tunnel to reach it.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: When we woke up at the Hotel there was no water for us to have a shower with, so we told the manager but still there was no water although we could get enough to do the washing with.  After a delicious lunch at the Marcopolo (sic) [Marco Polo Hotel] where we sat on carpets that covered cushions.  We went to the citadel and pretended that we had been staying with an Aunt.  While we were away Gengis Khan had come to the citadel and ruined it and killed all the people.  We visited the big buddha.  We wanted to climb to the back of buddha’s head but the gate was locked.  When we had climbed to the top of the mountain we found a watch tower with a super view of the valley and snow covered mountains.

entries.speaker: Mum
entries.text: Genghis Khan's grandson was killed in the city of Sighs so [he] decimated the entire city.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Halloween

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We woke up early and were driving by 5.45.  We followed a river through the mountains, and then left it to go through a valley.  Soon we were driving through hills again, and there was a light sprinkling of snow over everything, the road was very windy and bumpy, and we had a little engine trouble, it was very cold.  The snow got thicker as we climbed.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: After almost 3 hours, we saw some different looking mountains, and then the first of Band-i-amir’s great lakes, we drove on and were soon driving round them, stopping for photos every now and then, the lakes were very still and reflected the sky beautifully.  We were hoping to have a horse ride, but we couldn’t find anywhere where horses were being hired out.  We were just about to give up, when some boys came up on horses and told us that we could hire from the Hotel.  We drove up and hired 3 horses.  We had a super time riding round the lakes, F had never been on a horse before, and he cantered (a little bit) by himself.  My horse was worth 1500 Afs and was ridden in the Buzkashi which is a game with two teams of men on horses, a bit like football, but the ball is a goat, it’s a very rough game, but we hope to see a little bit, if possible.  We took the horses back, I cantered ahead, it was lovely.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We drove Fred up, and had lunch overlooking a beautiful lake, it rained a bit, so we packed up and started, earlier than we had been expected.  The road was wet and slippery, and it had been snowing again.  We came to one hill and it was all clay, so the wheels were spinning.  Mum and I got out to push, while F & H bounced inside to try and get the wheels to grip.  Mum and I got out two mats, we put them under the back wheels, and pushed some more, at last we got onto some stonier ground and Fred got moving by himself.  Mum and I were very muddy, and it started snowing again.  Dad drove quite a way to get out of the danger spot, so Mum and I had to walk a long way.  When we got there, Dad was putting some petrol from the jerry can into Fred, as we were using up a lot of it.  We drove on quite a way but the road was getting very wet and slushy; at last we felt the wheels spinning again. Mum and I jumped out, and started pushing, but to no avail.  The sky was very cloudy, but ther sun seemed to be shining over the lakes (grunt, growl).  We got the carpets out again, but the road was so wet, that they got just as slippery.  And the tyres spun so much on them, that they burnt.  We fixed ropes on the front and tried pulling, then Dad came and tried, I was freezing, ‘specially my fingers and toes.  After almost an hour we gave up, we had tried everything, we moved about 3m, and then nothing would budge us, except for creeping forward, an inch or so.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We got back in Fred, I just couldn’t warm up.  F made us some coffee.  We hoped that someone would come and tow, or push us, but no one did, we were thinking that we would have to spend the night there, when we heard the faint sound of an engine.  I thought perhaps that it was our imagination playing tricks, but soon a little Russian bus came into sight.  They needed some oil, so Dad got ours out, and while the man was fiddling with the engine, the other people helped push, with 6 strong people pushing, we only just got going.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: There were some tourists in the bus, they were very cold, the bus didn’t have a roof, so we lent them a sleeping bag, unfortunately, that was all that we could spare.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We arrived in Bamiyan after about 2 more hours driving, with no more mishaps.  We ate out at the ‘Marco Polo’ again.  When we had finished eating, they played the Sitar and the drum.  (Sitar is like this, it has 17 strings).  I didn’t like it much, because they kept on asking us to dance, and I was shy.  We slept in the ‘Zook Hotel’ again.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We are bogged. The hill is all muddy where the road is. So we are waiting. We got up early this morning and drove to the Lakes in Band-e-Amir. When we first arrived a lake stood before us. It looked as though someone had built a dam but it was not artificial.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: The lake had a lovely blue. It was quite dark, but had lovely white waterfalls gushing down to make lots of streams.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We hired some horses and rode round the lakes. It was lovely. I was a bit scared though when we rode near the edge of a gorge with a lake in and I cantered once or twice. My horse was worth 10 thousand afghanis (£140) – what a lot.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We are bogged in a snowy mountain.  We have been trying to get Fred up a muddy hill, wet with melted snow.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: This morning we woke up at 5 o’clock and drove to Bande-Amir which is a very small village and five lakes in a valley between snow-covered mountains.  We hired 3 horses and rode them to the top of a hill where we could see 3 lakes.  The farthest was a dark blue and the nearest was so clear you could see the bottom.  My horse was white.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: F & H went to get the bread in the morning for Mum & Dad, the children had porridge.  We went to do our diaries, in the restaurant, I talked to a nice French lady, F played with her daughter, Emanuelle.  We had chai at Marco Polo, then went to visit the ‘Small Buddah’, it was quite scary, climbing around the old caves.  We went up some very steep stairs to the head of the Buddah, some 115 feet high.  Some of the frescoes would have been lovely, if they hadn’t been so badly defaced.  After lunch, we climbed up to some different caves, we saw some lovely paintings, very small, but beautiful, we found some bits that had fallen onto the floor, and by mistake, I pulled a bit off, it had gold leaf on it.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We climbed the small Budda by the way of a staircase carved inside the rock. There were some windows to give light. Every two or three yards, well much more, there was what had once been a big cave but the front had fallen off at the top. We climbed right onto the Budda’s head. I was terrified there. H and I were 115 feet high with no rails at all. There was quite a nice view from the top of the Budda. D, Mum and Dad took some photos of the valley below us. (pic)

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Helena and I went on ahead. We found the remains of a cave; two walls and most of the ceiling were missing. On the remains of the ceiling there were some beautiful frescos. Some bits had gold leaf. They were the only faces we saw, because the Moslems destroyed faces of idols. the colours were still very bright; there were reds, greens, blues, blacks, whites, silvers, and gold leaf.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: This morning, F and I went to get the bread and on the way there I found a piece of cloth that was woven out of blue wool and silver and gold thread.  On the way back, we met a lovely little dog who was a goldish sandy colour.  We visited the small Buddha and climbed up some narrow (rather scary) stairs to the top of his head.  There was one place where I was really terrified - F had to encourage me a lot.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: Afterwards, F and I did some exploring on our own. We climbed to quite a lot of caves trying to get to a tiny Buddha.  We called Dad to help us down, and while we waited we started to build a platform of mud and stones.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36780 (9180 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Mum is ill.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Mum & Dad got the oil that we had lent to the bus back, we were still in bed when they went to get it.  After breakfast, we went to the local pump, we filled up the tank and did the washing up, the water was lovely and clean, it came straight up from a spring.  We left Bamiyan, drove to the ‘Red City’, we had lunch at some warm springs, they were a lovely temperature.  At the Red City, there were some little boys, they had some pretty crystals, some were tourmaline, they were all from the surrounding mountains.  We bought one, for 2 Afs, then parked Fred and started climbing, leaving Mum in the car.  There was a nice guard, he helped the children climbing off the paths instead of calling them down.  Some of the towers had beautiful brickwork.  It was tiring climbing.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We left Bamiyan to go to the Red City. On the turnoff next to a hotel we asked whether it was the right road; they told us it was and that it led to some hot springs. We decided to go to the hot springs first, because they were furthest away.  We were driving along when Dad heard the noise of water, but we couldn’t see it, so we got out and had a look. H and I went ahead and found the spring. Soon after, the others came in Fred. We had lunch and visited the Red City the rest …

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We left Bamiyan and drove to the red city.  We went 5km farther to some springs.  There were some hot and cold springs.  There was a very big river between some high rocky mountains.  Several times the river disappeared in to the rocks.  One pool, big enough to swim in, had concrete sides.  There were 2 very forcing hot springs in the pool which would push a stick up if you threw it in.  F and I found a toad (well I think it was a toad), it surprised us by hopping up the dry mountain.  After lunch we went to the red city.  We bought some tourmaline.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We camped just off the road, next to a very noisy river.  In the morning there was ice inside, on the windows, it was very cold.  Some nomads that we passed yesterday, walked by, with all their flocks, they must have been freezing.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We drove through some eerier, but very beautiful gorges until we came to Doab, there, we wanted to turn off to see the beautiful ‘Valley of Kings’ but the way was barred.  We found a Policeman, he took us to a house.  Upstairs was an old telephone and ??  ?? he found out that it would cost 10 dollars each, so we left it.  At lunch we dug caves and saw lots of camels.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: When we got up there was ice on the windows and it was very cold. H and I were sent out to play. We made stepping stones in the river. After we had breakfast some nomads passed us. We had seen them yesterday at Bamiyan.  We drove through a gorge. It had the most fabulous reds (iron ore) and turquoise with huge walls on either side. On two spurs of rock there were citadels that had been destroyed by Ghengis Khan. I thought they looked spooky and impossible to take.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: When we woke up there was ice inside Fred.  We drove along a river in a gorge and stopped for lunch by the river which had become very muddy.  After lunch, D, F and I started digging a cave community in a cliff.  While we were digging some camels came, among them were two very small ones.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We stopped for the night.  I went with F to dig mines.  In F’s mine there were lots of seams.  In mine, F found some coal and black seams.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 36932 (9332 miles travelled)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We stayed the night near some hills that were very easy to dig in.  F & H started mining, soon I caught the fever of the mad gold rush and was digging with them.  F found a small seam of what looked like coal (we don’t know what it really is).  I found some very fine gold adjust (well - near enough!).

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: When we left, we had to drive very slowly, as the road was just a dirt track.  We saw lots of things though.  There were some women, weaving on a horizontal loom, a big crowd of people round a boiling cauldron, dyeing (we think).  Mum waved to some ladies but a man with them shouted something very angrily.  We saw some wonderful horses.  In ‘Doshi’ we got onto a tarmac road, we drove much faster and couldn’t see anything as interesting.  We had to use the jerry can.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We drove most of Thursday and reached the bitumen road at last.

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 37099 (9499 miles travelled) Tash Gorgon

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: When we woke up, we were surrounded by camels.  We counted at least 70, but they were very spread out, and there were quite a few which we couldn’t see.  We could only see one man looking after them, someone later told us that they could be worth 10,000 Afs (£140).  That meant that the flock could have been worth about 700,000 Afs (£?!)

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We set out quite early, for Mazar, but we arrived in about two hours, instead of the calculated 4 to 5 hours.  We found out that, unfortunately, all the teams for Buzkashi were still in Kabul, so we couldn’t see it.  We found some of our friends - Ian and Viv - in their hotel, was a man who invited us for chai, we had some delicious fruit with ?? - the atmosphere was a little tense.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We camped in a little hollow, off the road, it was Guy Fawks night, so F & H collected some thistles, and made a pile, for a fire.  After dinner we lit it, and I put on a paper guy, everything burned very quickly.  We had some mint cake.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: In the morning, camel after camel slowly and casually sauntered past. They were black or brown or white or mixtures. Dad counted at least 70 camels, but there was only one man. A camel is worth about £140.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Then we drove on to Mazar-i-Sharif, hoping to see the buzkashi, national sport of Afghanistan, but they were at Kabul. We saw the Landrover of some friends of ours parked near a hotel. We went in and talked to them. Someone invited us for some chai. He came from round the Khyber pass and was a Patan. He bought Eagles for £210 pounds and sold them in Saudi-Arabia!

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We left Mazar-i-Sharif and camped. We are in a small dell in the hills. The ground is a sandy hard stuff with quite a lot of scrubby thorn plants about a foot high. It is Guy Forks, so Helena and I are gathering bushes to make a fire. There are no logs or fireworks, but we have got some big thistles for torches. The scrub burns well, so we have chosen a bare patch.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We woke up on Friday morning and found that we were surrounded by a herd of 70 or more camels, who seemed to be herded by only one man.  We left quite early to drive to Mazar-i-Sharif to see the buzkashi, which is a game played on horseback with a dead goat or calf as ball.  Unfortunately the buzkashi was not on as the teams were away in Kabul.  We met a Pathan(?) [Pashtun] from the Khyber Pass, he had come to buy eagles.  He had bought two and was sending them to Saudi Arabia, they were worth 15,000 AF each!

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 37239 (9639 miles travelled).  Below Salang tunnel

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 37335 (9735 miles travelled).  Kabul

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In the morning, we set off for Kabul.  We had to go through the ‘Salang Pass’, there was quite a bit of snow, it was 11,000 feel above sea level.  We went through a long tunnel (3kms long).

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We have not got very much water so we are rationing it.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We are going through the Sheba pass. At the top – 11,000 feet– there is a long tunnel through a mountain.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We suddenly found we had no water except half a gallon and today we are going through the Sheba Pass.  We have come to a snow shelter (of which there are many).  The next one is a long one.  Soon we came to a big tunnel.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We arrived in Kabul and went to the ‘Green Hotel’, Colin was there.  He had had dysentry, and had been quite ill.  We had dinner out with him at the ‘Sigis’, not very good.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In morning, F, H & I went shopping in Chiken Street.  After a lot of haggling, I bought a little waistcoat for Sasha (Zaza)?? 55 Afs down from 100.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We got to Kabul.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: D, F and I went shopping on our own in Chicken Street.  We went around the food shops and some of the fur shops in the food shops there.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We woke up at about 6.30am, F & H went to get the bread.  We went with Colin to see the ‘Kabul Museum’, the section on Bamiyan was very disappointing, we expected lots of beautiful frescoes, but there were only two large faded ones.  We saw some beautiful things there though, lots of inlaid guns, big and small, and lots of carvings.  After, we went to see the uncared for now, Babur’s garden, and Mum, Dad and Colin climbed to see the noon gun.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Our three-day stay in Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan. [PIC: Kabul all decorated!]

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We stayed in the green hotel near Chicken Street, where there are lots of shops. One shop, the old and new shop, had things bought from tourists. I liked one belt, with lots of pouches, which I thought went over the shoulder. The man said it was made from black leather and cost 600 afghanis. There were some good water bottles. The one I liked best had a metal case, which I thought would make a super survival kit, as the bottom could be used as a pan. But Mum and Dad said to wait till Australia.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We went to a shop called The Old and New Things Shop.  It had lots of things bought from other tourists.  There was a set with two goblets, a jug and a tray, all with blue and red jewels on them.  I bought one of the goblets with one red and one blue jewel on it.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: Dad, Mum and I looked everywhere, at last Dad and I found one that was nice, and cheap, 400 Afs (£5.87).  All had inside dark brown with white and brown embroidery on outside (pic).

entries.speaker: G/M
entries.text: Mileage = 37477 (9877 miles travelled).  Djellalabad

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We left the Green Hotel and started on the drive through the Kabul gorge to Djellalabad, we arranged to meet Colin at the toll gate, or Djellalabad.  The gorge was quite frightening, there were lots of short tunnels, coming out onto hair bends, every so often, there was a warning sign, with photograph of an accident on it, in some places, some wall had fallen and the road was crumbling away at the edge.  The Gorge was very bare and stony, after that was scrub desert and then suddenly Djellalabad appeared, lots of old trees, and orange trees everywhere.  It was all very lush.  Parked by the side of the road we saw Ian and Viv’s car, we stopped and we talked to them.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We found a nice campsite and soon, Colin rolled up!

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: In the morning we went to Hadda, with Colin in our car, it was quite interesting, but there were guards watching our every move, we could only walk on the wooden platform floor etc.. they were very fussy.  We saw some beautiful buddha faces.  We drove back and left Colin doing his Landrover, while we drove on to the border.  There, they didn’t search at all and we got through without any fuss.

entries.speaker: D
entries.text: We then drove onto Landi Kotal.  Dad, F & I went down to see the bazaar, which was supposed to have a big black market.  Dad asked if there was any alcohol, and a man said ‘No, but Hasheesh, Morphine and Cocain, in my shop’.  We drove on and came to Peshawar, at length we found ‘Deans Hotel’ we stayed there.  H & I had a lovely long bath.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: We went to [Familo] Hadda, there were lots of pillar-boxes decorated with Buddas. Some of the Buddas still had small red and blue jewels. Helena and I found men leaning out as if from battlements. They were about 5cms high and had shields, one of which still had stripes painted on it. At each corner there was a lion; the head at the very corner, the sides stretching in two directions.

entries.speaker: F
entries.text: Then we went through the Khyber pass [into Pakistan]. It has lots of concrete tank pillars by the side of the road and in the river bed. There were lots of built-in gun emplacements, you could hardly see the gun emplacements because they were little holes. There was a huge fort, but I could not see many soldiers. Many of the men wore rifles and bandoliers. I expected it to be more of a ravine. There were lots of memorials to battles that had taken place there.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: We stayed at a Hotel in Jellalabad.  So did Colin.  Francis and I found that we could get onto the wall by climbing a tree.  We were quite well shaded by it’s branches.  We found two palm branches about 3 metres long - they were very good for sweeping.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: In the morning, we went with Colin to Hadden.  Hadden was a room with lots of ruined bases of pillars which had lots of Buddhas carved on them.  I did not like it.

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: In the afternoon, we entered Pakistan and went down to the Khyber Pass.  On the Pass we saw a very pretty girl who had a small brother and sister - so we took a photo.  I found it disappointing .  We are in Peshawar staying at the Deans Hotel.  D and I bought a hankie which looks like this. (Pic)

entries.speaker: H
entries.text: In the Hotel, there is a sand pit, we played there with some new friends while the others went shopping.  We made a big city with many bridges and beginnings of gardens.
